extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, tax administrators, economists, and informed readers interested in public finance
extracted.subtask_description: General principles and practical standards for designing, administering, and evaluating taxes (customs, excise, local tolls, and other duties), with attention to revenue, equity, certainty, convenience, and prevention of smuggling. Derived from a classical political-economy treatment of public revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity, precision, and distinctness of tax laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax laws (especially customs book of rates) should be clear and unambiguous so contributors know what they owe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book of rates is extremely comprehensive and frequently uncertain under what article a particular sort of goods ought to be classed; mistakes sometimes ruin the custom-house officer and occasion much trouble, expense, and vexation to the importer. In point of perspicuity, precision, and distinctness, therefore, the duties of customs are much inferior to those of excise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine taxation to a few general-use articles when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: To have most contributors pay in proportion to expense, it is not necessary to tax every article; it is preferable to tax a few articles of general use and consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duties of excise are imposed upon a few articles only of the most general use and consumption. By confining customs to a few such articles and subjecting foreign manufactures to moderate taxes, revenue may be preserved while benefiting foreign trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use taxation as an instrument of revenue, not as a device for monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should be imposed to raise revenue, not to protect domestic producers or create monopolies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The taxes which at present subsist upon foreign manufactures... have, the greater part of them, been imposed for the purpose, not of revenue, but of monopoly. Taxation being always employed as an instrument of revenue, and never of monopoly, is the correct principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set tax rates to avoid reducing consumption (optimize for revenue)
rubrics_metrics.description: When revenue falls because consumption falls, the remedy is to lower the tax; the tax rate should be chosen to maximize revenue without unduly suppressing consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High taxes sometimes by diminishing the consumption of the taxed commodities ... frequently afford a smaller revenue to government than what might be drawn from more moderate taxes. When the diminution of revenue is the effect of the diminution of consumption, there can be but one remedy, and that is the lowering of the tax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tax policy to minimize smuggling (reduce temptation or increase difficulty)
rubrics_metrics.description: If revenue loss is from smuggling, remedy either by lowering the tax (reducing temptation) or improving administration (increasing difficulty of smuggling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the diminution of revenue is the effect of the encouragement given to smuggling, it may be remedied in two ways; either by diminishing the temptation to smuggle, or by increasing the difficulty of smuggling. The temptation can be diminished only by lowering the tax; the difficulty can be increased only by establishing that system of administration which is most proper for preventing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt administrative systems that limit evasion (excise-like administration for customs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs administration should, where feasible, follow excise practices (secure/public warehouses, officer inspections, certificates) to prevent smuggling and ensure correct duty payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importer might be allowed to carry goods to private warehouse (duties immediately paid) or public warehouse (no duty till taken out for home consumption). Public warehouses under custom-house officer key; dealers must be subject to visits and justify by certificates the payment of duty. Such a system increases difficulty of smuggling and could be extended to duties upon goods imported if confined to a few sorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid revenue leakage from drawbacks and export bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage drawbacks and export bounties carefully, as these can reduce neat revenue if they are effectively re-imported or are merely refunds of previous domestic taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What the revenue at present loses by drawbacks upon the re-exportation of foreign goods, which are afterwards re-landed and consumed at home, would, under this system, be saved altogether. Abolition of bounties upon exportation (unless genuine drawback of excise) would save revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of tax (who, what, when, and how much)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes should be certain in amount, timing, and person; uncertainty arises from inarticulate or unskilful legal expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such taxes ... may be perfectly certain; or may be assessed, so as to leave no doubt concerning either what ought to be paid, or when it ought to be paid; concerning either the quantity or the time of payment. Whatever uncertainty there may sometimes be ... cannot arise from the nature of those duties, but from the inaccurate or unskilful manner in which the law that imposes them is expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax luxuries rather than necessities (protecting the poor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes ought to fall on luxuries and not on the necessary expense of the inferior ranks, because taxing necessities ultimately burdens the superior ranks or reduces labour demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It must always be remembered... that it is the luxuries, and not the necessary expense of the inferior ranks of people, that ought ever to be taxed. The final payment of any tax upon their necessary expense would fall altogether upon the superior ranks of people; or lessen the demand for labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exemptions that benefit the wealthy unduly
rubrics_metrics.description: Privileges (e.g., exemption for brewing/distilling for private use) are unjust and cause the tax burden to fall disproportionately on the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fermented liquors brewed, and spiritous liquors distilled, not for sale, but for private use, are not in Great Britain liable to any duties of excise. This exemption ... occasions the burden of those duties to fall frequently much lighter upon the rich than upon the poor. Such exemption is surely most unjust and unequal, and ought to be taken away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate basis for local passage/tolls (bulk/weight vs value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local duties intended for maintenance (turnpike, canals) should be imposed according to bulk or weight; imposing them by value converts them into inland customs that obstruct interior commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those duties, when applied to such purposes, are most properly imposed according to the bulk or weight of the goods. When such duties are imposed... according to the supposed value of the goods, they become properly a sort of inland customs or excise, which obstruct very much the interior commerce of the country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transit duties can be legitimate when paid by foreigners
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties on goods merely transiting a territory (transit-duties) are acceptable sources of revenue when they are paid by foreigners and do not burden domestic industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some small states derive revenue from duties of this kind, which are paid altogether by foreigners. The most important transit-duty in the world is that levied by the king of Denmark upon all merchant ships which pass through the Sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider tax incidence and voluntary nature of taxed consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize who ultimately pays (consumers, not producers) and that consumption-based taxes are in part voluntary (people can choose not to consume).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such taxes... are paid finally, or without any retribution, by whoever consumes the commodities upon which they are imposed; yet they do not always fall equally or proportionally upon the revenue of every individual, because every man's humour regulates his consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience in time and mode of payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes that can be paid piece-meal in proportion to purchases are the most convenient for contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes upon luxuries generally are, and always may be, paid piece-meal, or in proportion as the contributors have occasion to purchase the goods upon which they are imposed. In the time and mode of payment, they are, or may be, of all taxes the most convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of collection / minimize net burden per revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxation should aim to collect revenue with minimal overall loss to the public (minimize the amount taken out of people's pockets relative to revenue raised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such taxes, in proportion to what they bring into the public treasury of the state, always take out, or keep out, of the pockets of the people, more than almost any other taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust tax structure holistically to reduce evasion (example: raise malt, lower distillery duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting the incidence within the tax system (e.g., higher malt tax but lower distillery duties) can reduce opportunities and temptations to smuggle and increase net revenue while achieving policy goals (e.g., discouraging spirits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By increasing the duties upon malt, and reducing those upon the distillery, both the opportunities and the temptation to smuggle would be diminished, which might occasion a still further augmentation of revenue. The abatement of taxes upon the distillery ought not to be so great as to reduce, in any respect, the price of those liquors (public-health objective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative accommodations to ease cash-advance burden on producers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where raising a duty causes a producer to have to advance more cash (e.g., maltster advancing tax), administrative measures like granting longer credit can remedy inconvenience without harming revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maltster might be obliged to advance a heavier tax, but whatever inconveniency might arise could easily be remedied by granting him a few months longer credit than is at present commonly given to the brewer.
